title: C++ containers for interviews
subtitle: Choose a container by the operation you need: lookup, last-in-first-out, first-in-first-out, smallest value or sorted search. These are foundations, not proof of interview readiness.

sections.title: Count with a hash map
points: `unordered_map<Key, Value>` stores a value for each key.
Lookup and insertion are average O(1), worst-case O(n). Use `find` to check membership without inserting.
sections.summary: Use a map when you need a value attached to each key.
sections.analogy: A tally sheet associates each number with how many times you saw it.
sections.gotcha: `counts[key]` inserts a missing key with a default value. `find(key) != counts.end()` checks without inserting.

sections.title: Track what you have seen
points: `seen.count(x)` is 0 or 1. An unordered set does not keep insertion order or sorted order.
sections.summary: Use a set for membership; use a map for key-to-value information.
sections.analogy: A guest list records whether a name is present, not how many times someone arrived.
sections.gotcha: Use std::set if sorted order is required; its lookup and insert cost O(log n).

sections.title: Stack: newest item first
points: `push` adds, `top` reads, and `pop` removes the newest item.
With the default container, these operations cost O(1).
sections.summary: Read top before pop: C++ pop returns nothing.
sections.analogy: Take the top plate from a pile.
sections.gotcha: Check empty() before top() or pop(). A stack does not let you access an arbitrary index.

sections.title: Queue: oldest item first
points: `front` reads the oldest item. `pop` removes it.
Use a queue for BFS. Default queue end operations cost O(1).
sections.summary: A queue visits items in the order they arrived.
sections.analogy: The first person in a waiting line goes first.
sections.gotcha: A queue is not a priority queue. Use deque when you need both front and back insertion/removal.

sections.title: Heap: choose the next extreme
points: A priority_queue gives the largest value by default.
`greater<int>` makes this a min-heap. Reading top costs O(1); push and pop cost O(log n).
sections.summary: Decide whether you need the smallest or largest value first.
sections.analogy: A priority line chooses the next item by priority, not arrival time.
sections.gotcha: A heap is not a fully sorted array. Only the top element is guaranteed to be the next extreme.

sections.title: Sort, then search
points: sort orders a vector in O(n log n). It changes the input order.
On a sorted vector, lower_bound finds the first value at least as large as the target in O(log n).
sections.summary: Check the sorting requirement and the end iterator before reading the result.
sections.analogy: Find the first shelf label that is not smaller than the label you want.
sections.gotcha: lower_bound may return end(). Do not dereference it. Sorting first can destroy original positions; store indexes if you need them.

exercises.explanation: The key 4 has count 2. There is one distinct key.
The set has two unique keys. 9 is absent.
pop removes the newest value, 9. The remaining top is 2.
The queue removes the oldest value, 2, leaving 9 at the front.

exercises.prompt: What is printed with the default priority_queue?
exercises.explanation: The default priority_queue is a max-heap, so its top is 9.
The first value at least 6 is 7, at zero-based index 2.
